extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying discrete mathematics / relations and orders
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and basic theorems about partial/total orders, bounds (least/greatest), minimal/maximal elements, and the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive closures of relations, aimed at readers learning discrete mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smallest element (of a family of sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element X of F is the smallest element of F iff ∀Y ∈ F (X ⊆ Y). Equivalently, a set being 'the smallest one with a certain property' means it has the property and is a subset of every set that has the property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used with the subset partial order. Example: the family F = {X ⊆ R | 5 ∈ X and ∀x∀y((x ∈ X ∧ x < y) ⇒ y ∈ X)} has smallest element A = {y ∈ R | 5 < y}. Note: a family may have no smallest element (see Example 4.4.7 part 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Largest and maximal elements (in a partially ordered set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a partial order R on A and B ⊆ A, b ∈ B is the largest element of B if ∀x ∈ B (x R b). b is a maximal element of B if there is no x ∈ B with (b R x and b ≠ x) (i.e., you cannot find a strictly larger element of B above b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions parallel those for smallest/minimal elements. Largest elements, when they exist, are also least upper bounds in many contexts (exercise/theorem connections explored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal and maximal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An element of B is minimal if no distinct element of B is strictly below it (no x ∈ B with x R b and x ≠ b). Maximal is defined dually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A family can have multiple minimal elements and then no smallest element (Example 4.4.10 part 2). Exercises ask to relate minimal/maximal to smallest/largest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower and upper bounds (Definition 4.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a partial order R on A and B ⊆ A, a ∈ A is a lower bound for B if ∀x ∈ B (a R x). a is an upper bound for B if ∀x ∈ B (x R a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lower bound need not belong to B — that is the only difference between a lower bound and a smallest element. Examples: 7 is a lower bound for C = {x ∈ R | x > 7} though 7 ∉ C; all numbers < 7 are lower bounds of C, and 7 is the greatest lower bound of C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound (l.u.b.) and greatest lower bound (g.l.b.) (Definition 4.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let U be the set of all upper bounds for B and L the set of all lower bounds. If U has a smallest element then that element is the least upper bound of B. If L has a largest element then that element is the greatest lower bound of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations: l.u.b. and g.l.b. Examples: For B = {1, 1/2, 1/3, ...} the l.u.b. is 1 and the g.l.b. is 0. Note: existence of l.u.b./g.l.b. depends on the ambient order (reals have completeness properties not shared by arbitrary partial orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound / greatest lower bound for subset partial order (Theorem 4.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the subset partial order on P(A) and a nonempty family F ⊆ P(A), the least upper bound of F is ⋃F and the greatest lower bound of F is ⋂F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies familiar set operations (union/intersection) with order-theoretic extrema in the subset ordering. Proof assigned in exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive closure (Definition 4.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation S ⊆ A×A is the reflexive closure of R ⊆ A×A if (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is reflexive, and (3) for every T ⊆ A×A, if R ⊆ T and T is reflexive, then S ⊆ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterizes the reflexive closure as the smallest reflexive relation containing R. Uniqueness follows from uniqueness of smallest elements when they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of reflexive closure (Theorem 4.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every relation R on A has a reflexive closure: S = R ∪ i_A (where i_A is the identity relation on A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show R ⊆ S, S is reflexive because i_A ⊆ S, and S is subset of any reflexive T containing R. Commentary emphasizes explicit construction and logical structure of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreflexive and strict partial/total orders (Definition 4.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is irreflexive if ∀x ∈ A ( (x,x) ∉ R ). R is a strict partial order if it is irreflexive and transitive. R is a strict total order if it is a strict partial order and satisfies trichotomy: ∀x∀y (xRy ∨ yRx ∨ x=y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: strict partial orders are not partial orders since they're not reflexive; antisymmetry is implied by the strict definition (exercise). Examples: 'proper subset' and '<' style relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric closure (Definition 4.5.4 and Theorem 4.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The symmetric closure of R is the smallest symmetric S ⊆ A×A containing R; it satisfies (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S symmetric, (3) if R ⊆ T and T symmetric then S ⊆ T. Explicitly S = R ∪ R^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: add, for each (y,x) ∈ R, the pair (x,y). Example with 'hates' relation: symmetric closure = {(x,y) | x hates y or y hates x}. Proof uses proof by cases and the minimality property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive closure (Definition 4.5.4 and Theorem 4.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitive closure of R is the smallest transitive S ⊆ A×A containing R (i.e., R ⊆ S, S transitive, and S ⊆ T for every transitive T with R ⊆ T). It exists and can be defined as ⋂{T ⊆ A×A | R ⊆ T and T transitive} (the greatest lower bound of that family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative constructive viewpoint: S consists of all pairs (x,y) for which there is a finite path from x to y by following R (reachability). The textbook notes the reachability construction is intuitive and that a full proof via that construction typically uses induction (deferred to later chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction via intersections of supersets (general closure method)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a property P (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), the closure of R with respect to P can be obtained as the smallest set S (when it exists) by taking the intersection of all supersets T ⊇ R that have property P: S = ⋂{T | R ⊆ T and T has property P}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for symmetric and transitive closures in the text; requires showing the family of such supersets is nonempty (e.g., A×A is always a reflexive/transitive/symmetric superset as appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric relations and relationships to strict partial orders
rubrics_metrics.description: R is asymmetric if ∀x∀y ((x,y) ∈ R ⇒ (y,x) ∉ R). If R is asymmetric then R is antisymmetric. If R is a strict partial order, then R is asymmetric (hence antisymmetric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises ask to prove these implications. This clarifies how various non-reflexive notions (asymmetric, irreflexive, strict) relate to antisymmetry and partial order properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of domain/range under closures (exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the symmetric closure S of R, Dom(S) = Ran(S) = Dom(R) ∪ Ran(R). For the transitive closure S of R, Dom(S) = Dom(R) and Ran(S) = Ran(R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are useful invariants when reasoning about what closures add: symmetric closure can expand domain/range by adding inverses; transitive closure preserves domain and range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships between different closures and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are various relationships and non-equalities between performing closures in different orders: e.g., transitive closure of symmetric closure vs symmetric closure of transitive closure need not be equal (exercises investigate S (sym then trans) and S' (trans then sym), showing S' ⊆ S but not necessarily equality). Also unions/intersections of closures across relations have specified containment relations (exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides exercises to explore which equalities/containments hold and counterexamples for failures. Useful caution: order of taking closures matters in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of closures (and smallest-element reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a closure (as 'smallest' relation with a given property containing R) exists, it is unique because smallest elements are unique when they exist (Theorem 4.3.6 invoked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies calling 'the' reflexive/symmetric/transitive closure rather than 'a' closure. Text uses smallest-element and greatest-lower-bound arguments to justify existence/uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as construction/verification patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Several worked examples illustrate how to find smallest sets with a property, symmetric/reflexive/transitive closures, and how to read closures from directed-graph representations (reachability for transitive closure, adding reverse edges for symmetric closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended proof strategies: define the candidate closure explicitly (e.g., R ∪ i_A or R ∪ R^{-1} or intersection of all transitive supersets), then verify the three clauses of the closure definition; use proof by cases for symmetric closure; use arbitrary-element-of-family arguments for intersection-based proofs.
